title: OpenAI forms independent math advisory group at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study
subtitle: Nine mathematicians — including Ed Witten, Timothy Gowers, Martin Hairer and Ravi Vakil — will advise on evaluating and communicating AI-generated math results, weeks after 25 Fields medalists warned labs were racing past the community.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI announced on September 21, 2026 the formation of an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. The nine founding members are François Charles, Camillo De Lellis, Timothy Gowers, Martin Hairer, Nikhil Srivastava, Ulrike Tillmann, Ravi Vakil, Edward Witten and Melanie Matchett Wood. The group operates independently of any AI company, members do not accept payment for the work, and it has no decision-making power at OpenAI. Its remit is narrow — assess the significance of emerging AI math results and advise on how those results are communicated.

The trigger is real friction. OpenAI claims that a single internal model has now resolved more than 100 additional open problems across most areas of mathematics, echoing earlier claims around Fermat's Last Theorem work, the Erdős model, and the Astra ten-open-problems announcement. Earlier in September, 25 Fields Medal-winning mathematicians signed an open letter arguing that AI labs are threatening their intellectual work by racing each other with press-release-driven solutions to famous problems. This advisory group is the first structural response.

The choice of the Institute for Advanced Study matters. IAS is not funded by OpenAI, employs Witten, and has hosted the community's most serious debates about mathematical priority and citation for a century. Putting the group there — rather than at OpenAI's own offices or a policy-adjacent think tank — is a deliberate move to inherit institutional credibility. The group cannot pace OpenAI's internal work, but it can withhold the community's assent from press claims, which is the coin of the realm in mathematics.

Takeaway for learners — communication matters more than capability once AI can plausibly touch open problems. A proof that has not been reviewed, formalized, or contextualized is not a proof — it is a claim. If you are studying math and thinking about AI, the frontier is not just whether a model can prove X, but who checks it, how, and how fast. Lean, Coq, and formal-verification tooling are becoming a bottleneck as important as the model itself. The advisory group's practical role will be to work out norms for that pipeline before the noise-to-signal ratio in the literature gets worse.
